one_line: Al Chen (Cisco) on shipping AI into five major banks in weeks rather than a year: CVE remediation with agent-run exploit tests, ClickHouse cross-region DR with data-correctness checks, and keeping PII/MNPI out of LLM-judge reasoning, with showing evidence as the main lever for compliance speed.
summary: Al Chen, who works on AI observability deployments at Cisco, describes what it takes to ship AI agents into production at large banks, where the stakes are regulatory and the timelines are long. He reframes the bottleneck as compliance velocity, which depends on showing evidence rather than asserting that a fix or control works. He covers three pillars: a build and image pipeline with CVE triage, multi-region disaster recovery for a ClickHouse-backed observability store, and preventing sensitive data leaks through LLM-judge reasoning traces. For each pillar he gives a concrete pattern: agent-run exploit tests in Harbor to verify CVE remediation, backup plus row-count and replica-convergence checks for DR, and a second redacted judge call to keep reasoning out of the UI. He argues that time-to-production is mostly set by internal process (image pull approvals, GPU sourcing, security reviews) rather than technology. The talk is practitioner-level and vendor-adjacent, but most claims come with specific operational detail.

key_ideas.idea: Bank production deployments are gated by compliance, not technology, and the way to speed them up is to show evidence of how each claim was verified.
key_ideas.detail: Speed comes from showing your work. Vendors who promise weeks rarely check against the customer's own infrastructure, security posture and cluster. Timelines stretch to months with formal security reviews, custom gateways or RBAC, and to indefinite delays without an image-pull approval process or a GPU sourcing story.

key_ideas.idea: CVE remediation across many banks is a multi-variable problem. Each bank runs different image versions, scanners and severity and SLA policies, so a one-off fix does not generalize.
key_ideas.detail: Each image carries many CVEs, and transient dependencies in open-source packages often cannot be fixed by the vendor. The team reads upstream release notes to justify why it is dependent on maintainers. Some banks want a newer package version, others want an older one with fewer CVEs.

key_ideas.idea: A version bump does not prove an exploit is gone from application code. Scanners like Sysdig, Wiz and Prisma only check the version number.
key_ideas.detail: The proposed check is an agent-run Harbor task: the agent gets the CVE and the claim that a newer version fixes it, then must write an exploit against the old version and a test that shows whether the new one still has it. Trials run in parallel on Docker, Modal or Daytona sandboxes, and results are aggregated across trials.

key_ideas.idea: The main database behind most AI observability tools (ClickHouse) has no managed cross-region failover, so banks must build DR themselves.
key_ideas.detail: Redis and Postgres have managed cross-region failover. The pattern described is: a backup job in the primary region writes to a bucket, and a restore job loads it into a DR region, with replica pods in that region. The backup tool is open source and maintained by Altinity, which competes with ClickHouse on managed operations.

key_ideas.idea: Backup logs prove a job ran, not that the data is correct. Check row counts across tables and confirm that replicas in a region have converged.
key_ideas.detail: Failure modes such as a bad disk, a bad node, a bad migration or replication lag can leave the restored data stale even when the job reports success. The takeaway is to verify data correctness, not just job status.

key_ideas.idea: Replication moves bytes freely, but data residency rules constrain where records live. The practical split is to replicate IDs and metadata across regions and keep the core trace data in the jurisdiction where it was created.
key_ideas.detail: Because a bucket does not care about geography, residency has to be handled deliberately at the architecture level.

key_ideas.idea: Redaction in the UI is not enough. LLM-judge reasoning can re-expose PII or MNPI that the UI appears to have removed.
key_ideas.detail: A judge prompt that asks for explanations so a human can verify the output can leak unredacted customer data into the reasoning field. Suggested fix: persist the score always, persist the reasoning only after a check confirms it has no sensitive data, and otherwise suppress it. The stronger option is a second judge that sees only redacted input, which doubles the LLM cost for that request.

key_ideas.idea: The guiding principle is that zero leakage and data sovereignty cost something real, and the cost is extra LLM calls and engineering work. Trust with security teams comes from showing the evidence and the reasoning behind each answer.
key_ideas.detail: The talk closes with the theme that showing work is the main lever on compliance velocity. A production checklist sits behind the three pillars, and the speaker offers to score deployments against it.

techniques.name: Agent-driven exploit verification for CVE remediation (Harbor task)
techniques.how: Model each CVE as a Harbor task. The environment holds the application's Docker image. The instruction tells the agent that the target package version supposedly fixes the CVE, and asks it to write an exploit against the old version, then a test that shows whether the exploit still works on the new version. Run many trials in parallel on Docker, Modal or Daytona sandboxes, and record pass/fail across trials as evidence.
techniques.when: A scanner reports a CVE is fixed by a version bump, but you need proof that the vulnerable code path is gone from your application, not just that the version number changed.

techniques.name: Cross-region ClickHouse DR with backup, restore and correctness checks
techniques.how: Run a backup job in the primary region that writes to a bucket with the open-source ClickHouse backup tool. Run a restore job that loads that bucket into a DR region, with replica pods there. After restore, compare row counts between tables and check that replicas within the region have converged. Treat the job's success log as necessary but not sufficient.
techniques.when: Your store has no managed cross-region failover, which is true of ClickHouse, and a regulator or bank requires a tested DR plan.

techniques.name: Split replication of IDs and metadata from core trace data for residency
techniques.how: Replicate only IDs and metadata to other regions so they can be looked up and routed. Keep the full trace payload in the region that the jurisdiction requires.
techniques.when: Replicating across regions for failover would otherwise move regulated records out of their jurisdiction.

techniques.name: Gating LLM-judge reasoning behind a sensitive-data check
techniques.how: Let the judge read raw trace data. Always persist its numeric score. Run a check on the reasoning field. If it is clean, persist the score with the reasoning. If it contains PII or MNPI, suppress the reasoning. For the strongest guarantee, run a second judge call whose input is already redacted and show its output in the UI.
techniques.when: Judges need to explain their scores for human review, but the explanations can contain sensitive data that the rest of the UI hides.

techniques.name: Audit the judge prompt, not only the UI
techniques.how: Read the system prompt of each LLM judge and the reasoning in the stored traces, looking for any line that invites the judge to quote or restate input data. Fix it at the source instead of relying on UI masking.
techniques.when: Before you claim a system is free of sensitive-data leakage.

numbers.claim: Bank production deployment timelines went from about a year down to a couple of weeks, according to the speaker's stated goal.
Timelines stretch to a few months with formal security reviews or a custom LLM gateway or RBAC. They stretch further when there is no image-pull approval process or no GPU sourcing plan.
Judge reasoning with a second judge on redacted input roughly doubles LLM calls for that request, because it adds one more LLM call per request.

hot_takes: Vendors who promise deployment in a few weeks usually have not checked that timeline against the customer's own infrastructure and security posture.
Scanner tools that only check package versions say nothing about whether an exploit remains in application code, and that gap should be closed with executable tests.
ClickHouse has no managed cross-region failover, so banks must own DR, and the speaker reads this as a real gap in the platform.
Redacting PII in the UI is not enough when LLM-judge reasoning can leak it on the backend, so the judge's own output needs its own control.

relevance.why: AgentOS L1 has a PII and prompt-injection scanner, and L2C Crucible has exec-gate guardrails and sandboxing. The talk's pattern of gating judge reasoning and verifying exploits with sandboxed agent tests applies to both, and ClickHouse is part of the L3 storage plan.
relevance.action: Add a check to the LLM-judge path so that judge reasoning is persisted only if a PII/MNPI scan passes, and keep the score regardless. Consider a Harbor-style sandboxed exploit test as an acceptance check for any CVE-remediation claim in Crucible.

relevance.why: The talk is about enterprise compliance for bank deployments and has no direct link to the Claude Code harness, checkpointing, planning or approvals.
